gallery.description:
The Royal Chapel and St. Joseph church is 
across from the Wellington Museum in Waterloo. With its distinctive green dome and lantern tower.
Consecrated more than 300 years ago in 1690, the chapel was restored in 1844 and again in 1968.

Make sure you see the beautiful oak wooden pulpit, rumored to be made by Antwerpian Van Hoof.

gallery.title: File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Saint Joseph's Church.jpg
gallery.description:
To visitors, Saint Joseph's church is now principally known as a shrine for the Twenty Seven Commemorative Tablets dedicated to British and Dutch victims of Napoleone Buonaparte. 
Saint Joseph's was initially built in 1687-1690 as "Royal Chapel" (royal, in honour of King Charles II of Spain), modified and expanded a few times over the centuries, one last time in 1855-1858 : on that occasion, all the commemorative tablets have been moved into the ailes, newly added to the nave.  

A first two, perfectly recognizable  ►(File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Saint Joseph's church, first commemorative tablets.jpg), had already been depicted in 1816 by James Rouse, while in the rotunda by then.  The tablets eventually numbered 27.

gallery.filename: 18 June 1815 – Victory at Waterloo – Lord Wellington's Bust, St Joseph's Church.jpg
gallery.title: File:18 June 1815 – Victory at Waterloo – Lord Wellington's Bust, St Joseph's Church.jpg
gallery.description:
Bust of Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington (1769-1852).  Signed and dated "G. G. Adams. Sc. // London. 1855" on the back. (Marble, ca. 60 cm)
George Gammon Adams (1821 – 1898), first a renowned medallist, became famous as portraitist-sculptor.  Having been chosen to take Lord Wellington's death mask, he created a first bust in 1852 for the 2nd Duke of Wellington (1808-1884).  So appreciated was it that G. G. Adams made several versions of it in the following years. 

One of them has been presented by the 2nd Duke of Wellington to Saint Joseph's Church : A l'intérieur du grillage qui ferme la partie méridionale du dôme, on voit, posé sur un socle de marbre, le buste de Wellington, en marbre blanc, qui a été donné par la famille de ce grand capitaine. (Tarlier)

The bust is now preserved in the rotunda : ►(File:18_June_1815_–_Victory_at_Waterloo_–_The_Duke.jpg).  The protective showcase is a later addition. 

In the Wellington Museum, across the street : another bust of Lord Wellington ►(File:18_June_1815_–_Victory_at_Waterloo_–_Draped_Bust_of_Lord_Wellington.jpg).
categories: Busts of Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington

gallery.filename: 18 June 1815 – Waterloo – St Joseph's Church, Tablet Left, 1.jpg
gallery.title: File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – St Joseph's Church, Tablet Left, 1.jpg
gallery.description:
The Commemorative Tablets to the Victims of the Battle of Waterloo.
Introduction. 
 A 1816 etching ►(File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Saint Joseph's church, first commemorative tablets.jpg) shows a first two tablets, easily recognizable (albeit depicted oversize) : the one on the left is now ►(File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – St Joseph's Church, Tablet Right, 1.jpg), and the one on the right is ►(File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – St Joseph's Church, Tablet Left, 8.jpg).  Both epitaphs are transcribed in full by Campbell (1817), being the "principal" among "some votive tablets" (those last ones not further documented).

By 1824, a nave had been added to the Rotunda, as shown on an anonymous etching ►(File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Saint Joseph's church, nave, 1824.jpg) which depicts several tablets neatly lined up, but unidentifiable.

By 1855 anew, two ailes had been added to the nave and the tablets, then numbering 27, were moved into these ailes. Their first comprehensive publication, by Tarlier & Wauters (1864), describes in-extenso 14 tablets on the left and 13 on the right.

Since that description, the tablets have been reorganized ; furthermore, two have been replaced by new ones to incorporate more names, and an additional two Dutch tablets have joined the original set. The total is still 27, i.e. 14 on the left and 13 on the right. 

Today, the Tablets to the British and Dutch Victims are now poorly crammed in the corners of the ailes, some at ground level, all behind rows of chairs – pitifully.

► Left aisle, 1st tablet : 
“Sacred to the Memory of the Officers, Non Commissioned Officers and Privates of the 2nd 30th Regiment of Foot 
Who Fell in the Battle of Waterloo.”


Victims of the napoléonic régime.

► Left aisle, 2nd tablet : 
Sacred To the Memory of ALEXANDER HAY Esquire of NUNRAW, Cornet in the 16th Light Dragoons, 
aged 18 years,  
Who fell gloriously in the memorable Battle of WATERLOO June 18th 1815.

O dolor, atque decus magnum !
Hæc te prima dies bello dedit, hæc eadem aufert ! –– (Æneis, Liber X, 507-8) 


Victim of the napoléonic régime.

gallery.filename: 18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Saint Joseph's church, nave, 1824.jpg
gallery.title: File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Saint Joseph's church, nave, 1824.jpg
gallery.description:
Anonymous lithography depicting the newly (1824) built nave, en-suite to the pre-existing Rotunda. Despite its new size, the church still kept being called : Chapel.  
Some Tablets dedicated to the British Servicemen fallen at Waterloo (18 June 1815) and Quatre-Bras (16 June 1815) are sketched, all neatly laid-out.  


[About thirty years later, two aisles would be added to the nave, giving the church its present day's architectonic aspect, and the tablets moved to these aisles.]

gallery.filename: 18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Wellington Museum, Edward Stables, tombstone tablet.jpg
gallery.title: File:18 June 1815 – Waterloo – Wellington Museum, Edward Stables, tombstone tablet.jpg
gallery.description:
Tablet recovered in 1990 from the tomb of Lieutenant Colonel Edward Stables (tomb fallen into oblivion at that time), now preserved by the Wellington Museum and affixed in the passageway linking the Chaussée de Bruxelles to the backyard of the Museum – (coordinates : 50.71762, 4.39822).
Tarlier & Wauters published Lieutenant Colonel Stables tomb in 1864 : (...) un beau sarcophage en pierre bleue, orné aux quatre faces de tablettes de marbre blanc. Aux angles sont quatre piliers en pierre bleue rattachés par des barres de fer.  Sur la face nord, dont la tablette est brisée, on lit les lignes suivantes, que nous avons complétées par conjecture : 
[Ben]eath this stone lies the [Body of] 
[lieutenant]-colonel Edward [Stables] 
[of Great Ho]rmeadbury in the [county of Herts.] 
[He served] in the contine[ntal Wars] 
[under Sir John M]oore and the Du[ke of Wellington,] 
[and was killed on the 18]th of June 1815 whil[st commanding a Battalion] 
[of Grenadier Guards] in the battle of [Waterloo] 
[at the close of] that mem[orable Day.] 
[He fell dist]ingui[shed] 
[By his Soldiers ble]st in his [Comrades tears.] 
[MDCCCXV]


Tarlier & Wauters pursue by describing the southern tablet (shown), whose text is integrally preserved.
